questions.text: A rough concrete wall looks much deeper when sunlight grazes it from the side. Which source-backed relationship explains the effect?

options.text: Texture affects how a surface reflects or absorbs light, and shadow can reveal the relief.
Texture affects only touch and never visual perception.
The effect proves the wall color has changed physically.
Only structural thickness can create shadow.

rationale.correct: TOA 2 defines texture as visual and tactile and links it to light reflection or absorption.
rationale.takeaway: Texture, light, and shadow work together in perception.
rationale.b: Texture is explicitly visual as well as tactile.
rationale.c: The perceived change can come from light and shadow rather than pigment change.
rationale.d: Openings and surface relief can also shape shadow.

questions.explanation: TOA 2 defines texture as visual and tactile and links it to light reflection or absorption. Texture, light, and shadow work together in perception.

questions.text: Which set of terms best matches the Batch 130 source map for describing color?

options.text: Span, load, shear, and moment.
Hue, value, temperature, and intensity or chroma.
Axis, datum, hierarchy, and rhythm only.
Rise, run, landing, and handrail height.

rationale.correct: TOA 2 names hue, value, temperature, and intensity/chroma as color descriptors.
rationale.takeaway: Color questions should use the source-backed vocabulary of hue, value, temperature, and intensity/chroma.
rationale.a: Those terms belong to structural behavior, not color perception.
rationale.c: Those are ordering principles, not the color descriptor set.
rationale.d: Those are circulation/accessibility dimensions, not color descriptors.

questions.explanation: TOA 2 names hue, value, temperature, and intensity/chroma as color descriptors. Color questions should use the source-backed vocabulary of hue, value, temperature, and intensity/chroma.

questions.text: A wall with deep three-dimensional openings casts alternating light, shade, and shadow across its surface. What is the safest interpretation?

options.text: The wall has no architectural effect because shadow is only absence of light.
The openings are articulating the wall by creating a texture of light, shade, and shadow.
The openings are relevant only if they are structural columns.
The pattern is a universal emotional code independent of context.

rationale.correct: TOA 2 states that three-dimensional openings can create a texture of light, shade, and shadows.
rationale.takeaway: Shadow can be an articulation effect when tied to openings, depth, and surface reading.
rationale.a: The source map treats shadow as a perceptual design effect, not just absence.
rationale.c: Openings can shape perception even when not columns.
rationale.d: Batch 130 avoids unsupported universal emotion claims.

questions.explanation: TOA 2 states that three-dimensional openings can create a texture of light, shade, and shadows. Shadow can be an articulation effect when tied to openings, depth, and surface reading.
questions.code_citation: Batch 130 local source map: TOA 1 lines 147-160; TOA 2 lines 544-575, 780-797, 2116-2132; Wiley official Ching record.

questions.text: A designer wants a form to read more visually heavy against its surroundings. Which color-related idea is source-backed?

options.text: Only floor area can affect visual weight.
Color is unrelated to light or visual perception.
Every warm color always makes a space socially successful.
Color can distinguish a form from its environment and affect visual weight.

rationale.correct: TOA 2 links color to visual perception and visual weight.
rationale.takeaway: Use color claims carefully: visual distinction and weight are safer than universal emotional promises.
rationale.a: Visual weight is not limited to floor area.
rationale.b: The source defines color as a light and visual-perception phenomenon.
rationale.c: The source map does not support universal psychological guarantees.

questions.explanation: TOA 2 links color to visual perception and visual weight. Use color claims carefully: visual distinction and weight are safer than universal emotional promises.
questions.code_citation: Batch 130 local source map: TOA 1 lines 147-160; TOA 2 lines 544-575, 780-797, 2116-2132; Wiley official Ching record.

questions.text: Why is flat, diffuse light likely to reduce the apparent depth of a textured surface compared with grazing light?

options.text: It removes all texture from the material permanently.
It changes hue into structural rhythm.
It softens the shadows that make surface relief legible.
It proves the surface has no tactile quality.

rationale.correct: Surface texture becomes legible through how incident light is reflected, absorbed, and shadowed.
rationale.takeaway: Lighting condition is part of how texture is read.
rationale.a: Lighting changes perception, not the material itself.
rationale.b: Hue and rhythm are different vocabularies.
rationale.d: The same surface can remain tactile even when less visually legible.

questions.explanation: Surface texture becomes legible through how incident light is reflected, absorbed, and shadowed. Lighting condition is part of how texture is read.
